title: Valuation: a good company at a high price

inOneLine.simple: Valuation compares the price with what you get for it. A great business can be a poor investment if you pay too much.
inOneLine.balanced: [[pe-ratio|P/E]] = price ÷ [[eps]]. Earnings yield = EPS ÷ price. [[dividend-yield|Dividend yield]] = dividend per share ÷ price. [[payout-ratio|Payout ratio]] = dividends ÷ net income. [[valuation|Valuation]] tools compare price with profit; they never say what the price will do next.

explain.simple: Knowing a company is good is only half the question. The other half is the price. The P/E ratio tells you how many years of today's profit you are paying for. A P/E of 12 means you pay 12 times one year's profit per share. Turn it upside down and you get the earnings yield: profit as a percentage of the price. The dividend yield and the payout ratio show how much of that profit comes back to you as cash.
explain.balanced: A high P/E means the price already assumes strong future growth. If the business does well but less well than assumed, the price can still fall. A low P/E means low expectations, which can be justified if profits are shrinking. P/E is meaningless when earnings are zero or negative, and it uses one year's profit, which may be unusual. These ratios are tools for asking questions, not signals to buy or sell.

assumptions: Price 6.80 USD; EPS 0.57 USD; dividends 87 and net income 114, millions of USD; 200 million shares
steps: Dividend per share = 87 ÷ 200 = 0.435 USD. Dividend yield = 0.435 ÷ 6.80 = about 6.4%.

assumptions: Same fictional company and the same business; illustrative scenario, not a forecast
Imagine the price rises to 22.80 USD with no change in the business
Profit then grows 2% a year for 5 years, and buyers later pay a P/E of 12 again
steps: Price at a P/E of 12 = 12 × 0.629 = about 7.55 USD.
That is about 67% below 22.80 USD. The business did fine; the price paid was the problem.

explainSimpler: Good company and good price are two separate questions. P/E tells you how much you are paying for each dollar of today's profit.
commonMistake: Assuming a great company is a great investment at any price. If the price already assumes more than the business later delivers, the investment can lose money while the company does well.

quickCheck.prompt: Price 15.00 USD, EPS 0.60 USD. What are the P/E and the earnings yield?
Two fictional firms are equally good businesses. One has a P/E of 10, the other a P/E of 50. What follows?

options.text: The P/E 50 firm is the better business
options.explanation: No: a high P/E reflects expectations, not proven quality.

options.text: Both are equally good investments right now
options.explanation: No: paying five times more for the same profit changes the outcome.

options.text: The P/E 50 price assumes much more growth
options.explanation: Right: if that growth does not arrive, the price has further to fall.

quickCheck.prompt: A company made a loss this year. What is its P/E?

options.text: Not meaningful, as earnings are negative
options.explanation: Right: P/E needs positive earnings; with a loss, it tells you nothing.
No: a P/E is not zero when there is a loss.
No: there is no meaningful P/E without positive earnings.
